item.title: Elina Gunawardena walks the Victoria’s Secret runway
item.description: Signed by a Sri Lankan agency at 14, she has walked in Paris and covered Vogue Netherlands. On Sunday in Los Angeles she walked the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show, and Sri Lanka is calling her the first of its models to do it.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
Some careers announce themselves slowly. Elina Gunawardena’s began in a Colombo agency at fourteen, because her older sisters had signed there first. Five years later, on Sunday 18 October, she walked the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show in Los Angeles, a show streamed free to the world on YouTube.

Sri Lankan media, including the Daily News and Newswire, are celebrating her as the first Sri Lankan model to walk the Victoria’s Secret runway. Victoria’s Secret’s own press gallery confirms her place in the show. She walked twice: in the Vintage Victoria segment, in a custom vintage VS tank, skirt and cardigan, and again in the Autumn Changes segment.

14her age when a Sri Lankan agency signed her, in 2021
2segments she walked in the show

A start at home

Her path began with Panthera Management in Sri Lanka, she told India’s t2 in April. Her sisters had joined the agency first, and Elina followed. Within months Ford Models Paris had taken notice. Her first major shoot was a cover for Vogue Netherlands.

Through it all, she said, her mother came to her shoots and travelled with her to Paris, and she credits her agents in Sri Lanka, Paris and London, her sisters and above all her mother for guiding her.

From Paris to Los Angeles

Since then she has walked for fashion houses including Hermès, Fendi, Emporio Armani and Max Mara. Her models.com profile lists more than 50 runway shows, among them the spring/summer 2027 collections of Givenchy, Dolce & Gabbana, Alexander McQueen and Simone Rocha. She is now represented by The Lions in New York, Ford Models in Paris and Storm in London.

She has said she is proud to represent Sri Lanka. On Sunday, she did it on one of fashion’s most watched stages, and she earned her place there the way every model does: show by show, client by client.

On a runway full of famous faces

Elina shared the stage with some of the most recognised names in fashion. In the Vintage Victoria segment she walked alongside Irina Shayk, Barbara Palvin and Precious Lee, and in Autumn Changes alongside Liu Wen, Elsa Hosk and Alex Consani, according to Victoria’s Secret’s official run of show.

  • Bella Hadid opened the show and Adriana Lima closed it. Kylie Jenner, Gigi Hadid, Candice Swanepoel, Behati Prinsloo, Doutzen Kroes, Alessandra Ambrosio and Rosie Huntington-Whiteley also walked.
  • Sport crossed over too: US footballer Trinity Rodman and Natalia Bryant walked in the PINK segment.
  • The music came from KATSEYE, Megan Moroney, Megan Thee Stallion and Tate McRae.

The show was created by Bureau Betak, with makeup led by Pat McGrath and hair by Guido Palau.

Melbourne on the same runway

She was not the only face from our part of the world. Ayen Agany, an Australian-South Sudanese model scouted in Melbourne, made her Victoria’s Secret debut in the same show, according to Victoria’s Secret’s press gallery and RUSSH.

Watch the show

The full show is free on Victoria’s Secret’s official YouTube channel.

Watch on YouTube ↗ · Angels Among Us docuseries ↗

Sources: Victoria’s Secret Press Room, Fashion Show 2026 runway gallery, official run of show and production credits; models.com; t2, 27 April 2026; Daily News; Newswire; RUSSH. Photo provided by Victoria’s Secret for editorial use.

item.title: Australia is Sri Lanka’s fourth-biggest source of visitors so far this October
item.description: New official figures show 77,868 tourists arrived in the first half of the month. India is far ahead, and Australia sits in fourth place.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
Sri Lanka welcomed 77,868 international tourists between 1 and 15 October 2026, according to the latest weekly arrivals report from the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA).

India was again by far the largest market, with 29,323 visitors, almost 38 per cent of the total. China (5,988) and the United Kingdom (5,291) came next. Australia was fourth with 4,187 arrivals, roughly one in every 19 visitors. Germany, Russia, France, Pakistan, the United States and the Maldives rounded out the top 10.

Since 1 January, 1,771,547 tourists have arrived in Sri Lanka. Australia is fifth for the year with 91,176 visitors, behind India, the UK, China and Germany.

77,868arrivals, 1–15 October
4,187from Australia, fourth after India, China and the UK
1,771,547arrivals in 2026, to 15 October
2,362,521arrivals in 2025, the record year

What the numbers tell us

These points are The Dosage’s own calculations from the SLTDA figures:

  • Sri Lanka averaged about 5,190 arrivals a day in the first half of October.
  • If that pace held for the whole month, October would finish at around 161,000 visitors. That is a little below the 165,193 recorded in October 2025. SLTDA has not published a same-period comparison, so treat this as a rough guide only.
  • The 2025 full-year total was 2,362,521. To match it, Sri Lanka needs about 591,000 more arrivals between 16 October and 31 December. That works out to about 7,675 a day, well above the current pace.

Why it matters to you

  • If you have family in tourism: Hotels, guesthouses, drivers, guides and restaurants rely on these numbers. A steady flow from Australia is good news for businesses that host Australian travellers.
  • If you are planning a trip home: The report counts arrivals only. It says nothing about fares or room rates, so compare prices early if you are travelling for the December and January holidays.
  • If you follow Sri Lanka’s economy: Visitor numbers are one of the quickest monthly signals of how the recovery is tracking. Watch for SLTDA’s full October figures.

Sources: Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority, Weekly Report 1st to 15th October 2026; SLTDA Weekly Tourist Arrivals Reports 2026.

item.title: The price of a full tank
item.description: A war in the Gulf, damaged refineries in Russia and a tax that came back. How fuel got this expensive in Melbourne and Colombo, and what you can do about it.
item.dc:creator: Eashaan Dassanayaka
item.content:encoded:
Every oil shock follows the same script. In 1973, during a war in the Middle East, Arab members of OPEC placed an oil embargo on several countries. The price of a barrel first doubled, then quadrupled, and cars waited in long lines for petrol. The embargo held until March 1974. The lesson stuck: when supply is threatened at a single point, the whole world pays.

In 2026, that point is the Strait of Hormuz. When war broke out in the Gulf region on 28 February, the world’s busiest oil route became a war zone.

1. The narrow door

In 2024, about 20 million barrels of oil a day passed through the strait, the narrow sea lane between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula. That was about a fifth of all the oil the world used. In September 2026, flows through the strait were 10.9 million barrels a day, the IEA says: just over half the 2024 level.

Explainer

The Strait of Hormuz, in numbers

The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow channel of sea between Oman and Iran. It links the Persian Gulf, where many of the world’s biggest oil producers sit, to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea, and from there to the rest of the world. It’s deep enough for the largest oil tankers. For most of the oil and gas shipped out of the Gulf, it’s the only way out by sea.

21miles wide (about 34 km) at its narrowest point
2miles: the width of the shipping lane each way, with a 2-mile buffer between them
20mbarrels of oil a day went through in 2024
1 in 5of every barrel the world used in 2024, and more than a quarter of all oil traded by sea
1 in 5of the world’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) trade, mostly from Qatar
84%of the crude oil went to Asia. China, India, Japan and South Korea took 69%

Who ships through it

Saudi Arabia ships more crude through the strait than any other country: 38% of the crude that passed through in 2024, about 5.5 million barrels a day. Iraq, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Qatar and Iran also depend on it.

What happens when it’s disrupted

Even a short disruption can delay supply, raise shipping costs and push up energy prices around the world, the US Energy Information Administration says. There are only two real detours: Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, and the UAE’s pipeline to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman. Together they have about 2.6 million barrels a day of spare room. That covers roughly one barrel in eight of what normally goes through the strait.

That’s why the September 2026 figure matters. Flows through the strait were 10.9 million barrels a day, the IEA says: just over half the 2024 level. Because so much of the oil heads to Asia, Asian refineries feel it first, and their fuel prices ripple out to every country that buys from them.

Sources: US Energy Information Administration, Strait of Hormuz (16 June 2025) and world oil transit chokepoints (4 January 2012); IEA, Oil Market Report, October 2026. Shares and conversions are our calculations.

Freeze frame

Picture a stadium with five exits. Close one of them, and everyone still gets out eventually. But nobody walks calmly. They push.

Oil traders are the crowd. When one exit closes, they don’t wait to see how bad it gets. They pay more now, in case it’s worse tomorrow.

2. The fever chart

Brent crude, the benchmark for most of the world’s oil, closed at US$71.32 a barrel on 27 February. By 7 April it was US$138.21, almost double. Then it fell all the way back. On 2 July it closed at US$68.53, below its pre-war level.

It didn’t stay there. Military strikes resumed on 7 July, according to the US Energy Information Administration, and in September oil tankers and pumping stations on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline came under attack. On 14 October Brent closed at US$126.55. The same day, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that “renewed attacks in the Gulf leave the recovery fragile.”

3. Why diesel costs more

In Melbourne, diesel averaged 281.8 cents a litre in the week to 11 October, against 240.4 cents for unleaded. That’s a gap of about 41 cents.

The IEA points to two causes. Shipments of refined fuel from the Middle East were 1.9 million barrels a day in September, still below half their pre-war level of 4.7 million. And damage to Russian refineries during the war in Ukraine has cut their diesel output. Together, lost diesel exports from Russia and the Middle East came to 1.3 million barrels a day, only partly made up by other suppliers. Wholesale diesel reached record highs of around US$220 a barrel in Europe and the United States in September, and the IEA expects the market to stay tight well into 2027.

Freeze frame

Think of the world’s fuel supply as a bathtub. Tankers and refineries fill it, and every car, truck and generator drains it. Since February, the taps have run slower than the drain.

By the end of September, global oil stocks were 509 million barrels lower than at the end of February, the IEA says, and stocks held on land were at their lowest since at least 2016. With so little in reserve, each new disruption moves the price further.

4. The tax that came back

Australia added a local twist. On 30 March, the federal government halved fuel excise, the tax built into every litre. With the states agreeing to hand back their extra GST from higher fuel prices, the total cut came to 32 cents a litre from 1 April to 30 June. From 1 July a smaller 16-cent cut applied. On 2 August it ended.

Excise is back at its full rate, now 53.7 cents a litre after its regular August increase. Add GST, and nearly a third of what you pay at the bowser is tax.

5. Colombo and Melbourne, side by side

In Sri Lanka, the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation announced a price revision from midnight on 30 September, the Daily Mirror reported: Petrol 92 went up Rs 15 to Rs 414 a litre, Auto Diesel Rs 10 to Rs 392 and Super Diesel Rs 50 to Rs 528. Petrol 95 stayed at Rs 475 and kerosene at Rs 285. At about Rs 230 to the Australian dollar (People’s Bank, 16 October), here’s how a litre compares:

Rs 414Petrol 92 in Sri Lanka (about A$1.80)
A$2.40Unleaded 91 in Melbourne (about Rs 554)
Rs 392Auto diesel in Sri Lanka (about A$1.70)
A$2.82Diesel in Melbourne (about Rs 650)

At the pump, Colombo is cheaper. Against wages, it’s the other way round. Sri Lanka’s minimum wage is Rs 1,200 a day, which buys 2.9 litres of petrol. Australia’s is A$1,004.90 for a full-time week; a day’s share, A$200.98, buys about 84 litres in Melbourne. Even so, an 80-litre diesel tank in Melbourne costs about A$225.

6. What you can do

See every price before you drive. Servo Saver, in the free Service Victoria app, shows live prices at more than 1,200 service stations. Each station’s maximum price is set for 24 hours from 6am, and tomorrow’s is published by 4pm. If tomorrow is higher, fill up tonight. How Servo Saver works

Lock a price for a week. The My 7-Eleven app’s Fuel Price Lock holds the best nearby price for 7 days, for up to 150 litres. It saves you up to 25c a litre. Fuel Price Lock terms

Check your energy company’s app. EnergyAustralia electricity and gas customers get 6c a litre off at 7-Eleven, up to 100 litres a fill, by scanning a barcode in the EnergyAustralia app. It can’t be used together with a price lock. Other energy companies, banks and motoring clubs run similar deals, so check yours. Offer terms

Leave the car, take the train. All Victorian public transport, metropolitan and regional, is half price until 1 January 2027, including V/Line seat bookings. For a show in the city, that can cost a fraction of the fuel. Half-price travel

Sources: US Department of State, Office of the Historian, Oil Embargo, 1973–1974; US Energy Information Administration: Strait of Hormuz (16 June 2025), third-quarter oil prices (5 October 2026) and Europe Brent Spot Price FOB, daily; IEA, Oil Market Report, October 2026 (14 October); Prime Minister of Australia media releases, 30 March, 2 April and 21 June 2026; Australian Taxation Office; Australian Institute of Petroleum, weekly petrol and diesel reports, week ending 11 October 2026; Ceylon Petroleum Corporation fuel price revision, as reported by the Daily Mirror (Chaturanga Pradeep Samarawickrama, 30 September 2026); Fair Work Ombudsman; National Minimum Wage of Workers (Amendment) Act, No. 11 of 2025; People's Bank; Consumer Affairs Victoria, Servo Saver and price reporting rules; 7-Eleven; EnergyAustralia; Transport Victoria. Conversions and comparisons are our own calculations. Offers can change, so check the terms before you rely on them. The Dosage has no commercial arrangement with any company named.

General information, not financial advice.

item.title: Elon Musk joked his new car could detach your retina. Could it?
item.description: Tesla says its flying Roadster will only get quicker, up to the limit of the human body. We checked what eye science says about that limit.
item.dc:creator: Eashaan Dassanayaka
item.content:encoded:
Tesla has finally unveiled its second-generation Roadster, nine years after it was first promised. At a launch at SpaceX’s rocket test centre in McGregor, Texas, near Waco, on 15 October, the car hopped over a row of other vehicles on compressed-air thrusters and, in a live run, went from 0 to 96 km/h (60 mph) in 0.81 seconds.

Then Elon Musk said the production car would be even quicker. Citing Newton’s second law, he said more force and less mass would mean more acceleration. How much quicker? Tesla would, he said, “ride the limit of don’t detach the retina” of the person inside.

It was a joke. But it sets an unusual target: a car limited by the human body, not by its motor. So we looked at the science.

What 0.81 seconds does to you

Reaching 96 km/h in 0.81 seconds means an average push of about 3.4 g, more than three times your body weight pressing you back into the seat. Tesla says its top “Rocket” version will do it in under 0.59 seconds, a claim not yet shown in public. That works out to about 4.6 g on average, with brief peaks higher.

3.4 gAverage force in the 0.81-second live run (our calculation)
4.6 gAverage force if the “Rocket” version hits its claimed 0.59 seconds
Mach 0.5Musk’s top-speed goal, about 617 km/h
2028Tesla’s target for starting production

Which way the force pushes matters most

Pilots and astronauts have been tested for decades, and the main lesson is that direction matters. When g-force runs from head to toe, as in a fighter jet’s tight turn, blood drains away from the eyes. NASA research found untrained people start losing side vision at about 4.1 g and black out at about 4.7 g.

A car launch pushes you from chest to back instead, and the body copes far better. NASA research puts the seated limit for sustained chest-to-back g at about 8 g, and the limiting factors are breathing and chest pain, not eyesight. In very short pulses, people have taken around 40 g for a quarter of a second.

How the Roadster’s launch compares

Average g-force, chest-to-back unless noted, drawn to scale.

Tesla Roadster (our calculations)Human tests (NASA, US Air Force, published research)
Roadster “Performance” (claimed under 1.6 s)
1.7 g
Roadster live run (0.81 s)
3.4 g
Roadster “Rocket” (claimed under 0.59 s)
4.6 g
Head-to-toe blackout, untrained (for comparison)
4.7 g
Seated chest-to-back, sustained limit
8 g
Brief chest-to-back pulse (about 0.25 s)
40 g
John Paul Stapp’s rocket-sled stop, 1954
46.2 g

These figures act in different directions and for different lengths of time, so they give a sense of scale, not interchangeable human limits.

Side note

Speed doesn’t hurt. Acceleration does. Just ask a fighter pilot.

The fastest crewed aircraft ever flown, NASA’s rocket-powered X-15, reached 4,520 mph (Mach 6.7) in 1967. The SR-71 Blackbird spy plane cruised at up to Mach 3.3. At a steady speed, though, the body feels nothing at all, which is why airline passengers can eat lunch at cruising speed. What strains the body, and the eyes, is changing speed or direction quickly.

That’s why fighter pilots worry most about g-force. An F-16 can pull up to 9 g in a hard turn, which tries to drain blood from the head. The first warning is “light loss”: vision dims and narrows before the pilot can pass out. Pilots fight it in three ways:

  1. A g-suit. Air bladders inflate around the stomach and legs. The US Air Force says the squeeze forces blood “up toward your cranium” to help keep vision and consciousness.
  2. The straining manoeuvre. Pilots tense their legs, buttocks and stomach, and take a quick breath about every three seconds, to keep blood pressure up in the head.
  3. A tilted seat. The F-16’s seat leans back 30 degrees instead of the usual 13, which the US Navy says improves g tolerance.

Notice that none of this is about the retina coming loose. For pilots, the danger to the eyes is blood leaving them. That’s the opposite direction to a car launch, which presses you back into your seat.

So can acceleration detach a retina?

The retina is the thin, light-sensing layer at the back of the eye. A detachment happens when it peels away from the tissue that supports it. It’s an emergency that can cause permanent vision loss.

Doctors have documented cases linked to acceleration, from roller coasters rather than cars. In 2024, eye specialists in Toronto reported two young women whose retinas detached after roller-coaster rides. Both already had risk factors: one had a family history of detachment, and the other was very short-sighted with weak areas of retina. Reviewing other reported cases, the authors concluded that a “structural predisposition is likely necessary.” In eyes without that weakness, similar forces caused bleeding, but not detachment. Two cases show a possible link, not proof, and they say nothing directly about a car.

Cases like these are rare. Answering a reader’s question for the American Academy of Ophthalmology, ophthalmologist Dr Richard Bensinger said roller coasters are “unlikely” to be a problem for short-sighted people.

The most extreme human test on record is US Air Force doctor John Paul Stapp’s. In 1954 he rode a rocket sled to 632 mph (about 1,017 km/h), then stopped in 1.4 seconds, taking 46.2 g. Almost all the tiny blood vessels in his eyes burst, and he feared his retinas had detached. He was temporarily blinded and left hospital the next day, but his eyesight was never quite the same. His was a sudden stop, not a launch, so it isn’t a safe or unsafe limit for a car; it shows how far human tests have gone.

Our verdict

No one has set a g-force at which a retina detaches. Force direction, how long it lasts and the state of the eye all matter. There is currently not enough evidence to show that the Roadster’s reported acceleration would cause retinal detachment in an otherwise healthy eye. For an eye that’s already vulnerable, the reported cases are rare, but they suggest a hard launch could matter, whether it comes from a roller coaster or a hypercar. So Musk’s joke points at a real risk, but the evidence doesn’t show it for most people at these speeds.

“The production car will actually do better than that.” Elon Musk, at the launch

Why it matters to you

  • Know your risk. Retinal detachment is more likely if you’re very short-sighted, have a family history of it, have had eye surgery such as cataract removal or a serious eye injury, or are aged about 40 to 70.
  • Before extreme rides such as launch roller coasters, theme-park thrill rides or track experiences, ask your eye doctor if any of those apply to you.
  • Know the warning signs: a sudden shower of floaters, flashes of light, blurred vision, or a curtain-like shadow over your vision. These need care right away. It’s painless, so don’t wait. In Australia, see your GP or optometrist the same day, or go to an emergency department. In Sri Lanka, go to the nearest hospital eye unit.
  • The car itself: Tesla is aiming to start production in 2028. It is taking reservations of US$50,000 to US$250,000, TechCrunch reported, and Musk said the car may not be legal in all places, so the thruster versions may never be road-legal in Australia or Sri Lanka.

How we worked it out: average g = 26.8 m/s (60 mph) ÷ time ÷ 9.81 m/s². These are average accelerations worked out from Tesla’s claimed times, not measured forces on the driver and not injury thresholds; peak forces will be higher. The human tolerance figures come from controlled tests and vary from person to person.

Sources: Tesla Roadster launch, 15 October 2026 (Tesla livestream); TechCrunch; Pickel et al., “Roller Coasters and Retinal Detachment”, Case Reports in Ophthalmology, 2024; American Academy of Ophthalmology; NASA Technical Reports Server, “Acceleration”; NASA, X-15; Smithsonian, SR-71; US Navy, F-16; US Air Force Safety Center; The Space Review; Airman magazine and Wright-Patterson Air Force Base; Mayo Clinic.

General information, not medical advice. If you have symptoms, get medical help straight away.

Editorial review · 16 October 2026

How we checked this story

  • Checked against Tesla’s livestream: Musk’s quotes, the 0.81-second run, the venue and the 2028 production target.
  • Our calculations: the 1.7 g, 3.4 g and 4.6 g figures are averages worked out from Tesla’s claimed times, not measured forces on the driver.
  • Medical and historical sources: a 2024 case series in Case Reports in Ophthalmology, NASA acceleration research, and US Air Force records on John Paul Stapp.

AI tools helped with research and a preliminary review. The Dosage editorial team made every final decision. No endorsement by any AI company is implied.

What Grok (xAI) said when we asked it to review this story on 16 October 2026:

  • Does the article fairly represent Musk’s retina comment? “Yes.”
  • Is any statement about Tesla or Musk inaccurate or unfair? “No major inaccuracies or unfairness.”
  • “Overall the draft is careful, evidence-based, and fair.”

item.title: Half-price trains, trams and buses: what you’ll pay, and how to tap with your bank card
item.description: Public transport across Victoria is half price for everyone until 1 January 2027. Here’s the new daily maximum, how tap and go works, and what concession holders need to do first.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
Public transport fares in Victoria have been half price since 1 June, and the discount runs until 1 January 2027, according to Transport Victoria. You don’t need to sign up for anything: the half-price fare is charged automatically when you touch on.

$5.70full fare daily maximum (was $11.40)
$2.85concession daily maximum (was $5.70)

What’s covered, and what isn’t

The discount applies to metropolitan trains, trams and buses, and to regional trains, coaches and buses, including town bus services. It does not apply to SkyBus, ferries or regional buses that aren’t subsidised by the government. Concession fares, for students and seniors for example, are halved again.

No myki? Use your bank card or phone

You can now pay with a Visa or Mastercard debit or credit card, or a phone or smartwatch, on trains, trams and myki-enabled buses. Transport Victoria says tap and go fares are the same as myki fares.

  • Tap on and off with the same card or device.
  • Take your card out of your wallet before tapping, so the reader doesn’t pick up the wrong one.
  • Charges can take up to three days to appear in your bank account. You may see a pending amount first.

If you have a concession card

Don’t just tap your bank card. Transport Victoria says concession holders must first link a contactless payment method to their concession entitlement. Until you’ve done that, keep using your concession myki so you’re charged the right fare.

Already free, still free

  • Early Bird: metro trains are free if you touch on and off before 7am.
  • Under 18s travel free with a Youth myki.
  • Seniors travel free on weekends.

Why it matters to you

If you’ve just arrived in Melbourne, or you’re a student, every trip now costs half the normal fare. Half-price fares end on 1 January, so it’s a good time to visit family across town or take a regional trip.

Sources: Transport Victoria, Public transport now half price for everyone (22 May 2026) and Tap and go, accessed 15 October 2026. Includes information © State of Victoria (Department of Transport and Planning), used under CC BY 4.0. Fares and rules can change: check transport.vic.gov.au before you travel.

item.title: Colombo or the whole country? Two ways Sri Lanka measures rising prices
item.description: Sri Lanka publishes two inflation figures every month. Which one matters depends on where you live and what you buy.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
When you hear that prices in Sri Lanka are rising 8% a year, there are actually two numbers behind the headline. Both come from the Department of Census and Statistics, and they don’t always move together.

8.0%Colombo prices (CCPI), year to September 2026
8.1%national prices (NCPI), year to August 2026

The two indexes

  • Colombo Consumer Price Index (CCPI): tracks prices in the urban areas of the Colombo District. It comes out at the end of each month, so it is usually the first figure you hear. The Central Bank uses it as its main measure of inflation.
  • National Consumer Price Index (NCPI): tracks prices across all provinces, from district towns all over the country. It comes out about three weeks after the month ends.

Why food makes the difference

Each index is built from a “basket” of what households actually spend money on. Families outside Colombo spend a much bigger share of their money on food.

  • Food makes up about 26% of the Colombo basket.
  • Food makes up about 39% of the national basket.

So when rice, vegetables or coconut prices jump, the national figure tends to feel it more. When fuel, electricity, transport or rent rise, the Colombo figure can move faster. In August, national food prices were up 6.6% on a year earlier and non-food prices 9.3%, the Department reported, a sign that this year’s rise is being driven mainly by energy and other costs rather than food.

What it means for you

  • In Colombo or another city: watch the CCPI. It is closer to your costs for transport, utilities and rent.
  • In a district town or village: the NCPI is the better guide, because food is a bigger part of your spending.
  • Sending money home from Australia: the family you support may be feeling food prices more than the headline figure suggests.

The next national figure, for September, is due in the third week of October.

Sources: Central Bank of Sri Lanka, Annual Report 2022, Box 6 (rebasing the consumer price indices); Department of Census and Statistics NCPI for August 2026, as reported by Newswire, 21 September 2026; CCPI for September 2026 (see our story on prices and the Central Bank). This is general information, not financial advice.

item.title: Vap Poya and Deepavali: two holidays coming up
item.description: Vap Poya falls on Sunday 25 October and Deepavali on Sunday 8 November. What each one marks, and how families celebrate.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
Two public holidays are coming up in Sri Lanka, both on Sundays this year, according to the government’s 2026 holiday calendar.

25 OctVap Full Moon Poya Day
8 NovDeepavali Festival Day

Vap Poya: the end of the rains retreat

Vap Poya marks the end of Vas, the three-month rainy-season retreat when Buddhist monks stay in one place to meditate and study. After Vap Poya, temples hold Katina ceremonies, where families offer a specially prepared robe and other requisites to the monks who kept the retreat. For many families it is one of the most meaningful almsgivings of the year, often planned for months.

Like every Poya, it is a day for temple visits, observing the eight precepts, and quiet time with family. Shops selling alcohol and meat are usually closed.

Deepavali: the festival of lights

Deepavali, also called Diwali, is celebrated by Hindus in Sri Lanka, most of them Tamil, and marks the victory of light over darkness and good over evil. Homes are lit with rows of small oil lamps, and the day often begins with an early oil bath, new clothes and a visit to the kovil (temple). Families draw colourful kolam patterns at the doorway, share sweets with neighbours and visit relatives.

Celebrating far from home

If you are in Melbourne or elsewhere abroad, both days fall on a Sunday this year, which makes it easier to join a temple or kovil near you. Check with your local temple for times, especially for Katina ceremonies, which are often held on weekends after Vap Poya.

Sources: Government of Sri Lanka, 2026 public holiday calendar; Ada Derana, 2026 holiday list. Customs vary between families and communities.

item.title: A new health hub opens on Flinders Street on Monday
item.description: GPs, counselling, drug treatment, meals and showers under one roof, opposite the station. Here’s what it offers, and why not everyone is happy.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
A new community health centre for some of Melbourne’s most vulnerable people opens on Monday 19 October on Flinders Street, opposite Flinders Street Station.

Flinders Street Health will be run by cohealth with $36.4 million from the Victorian Government, which announced the opening on 12 October. It is part of the state’s $95 million plan to reduce drug harm.

$36.4mfrom the Victorian Government
19 Octopening day, opposite Flinders Street Station

What’s inside

  • GPs and primary health care
  • Mental health and wellbeing support
  • Alcohol and other drug treatment, harm reduction and referrals
  • Counselling, and help with housing, jobs, family violence and legal problems
  • Meals, showers and other basic facilities

Harm reduction workers and nurses will also work from the hub across the CBD. cohealth and the Department of Health say they will work with Victoria Police and the City of Melbourne.

“Everyone deserves access to healthcare and support,” said Mental Health Minister Ingrid Stitt. Lord Mayor Nick Reece told the ABC it was “the biggest investment in community health in the central city in decades”.

Not everyone is convinced

Some traders and city councillors worry about anti-social behaviour in the area, the ABC reported. The Greens welcomed the hub but want more supervised injecting rooms, while the Coalition says it wants more detail on the hub’s scope and consultation. A trial of hydromorphone, an alternative to methadone, is due to start at the site in 2027.

Why it matters to you

Thousands of us pass through Flinders Street every day. If you know someone sleeping rough or struggling with drugs or alcohol, this is a new place in the city where they can see a doctor, get a meal and get help with housing, all in one visit.

Sources: Victorian Government, New Health Hub Supports Melbourne’s Most Vulnerable, 12 October 2026; ABC News, 12 October 2026. General information, not medical advice.

item.title: Ten years on from Melbourne’s thunderstorm asthma disaster, this season could be a bad one
item.description: A warm, wet winter means more grass pollen. People from Sri Lankan and South Asian backgrounds were hit hard in 2016. Here’s how to stay safe.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
Victoria’s thunderstorm asthma forecasting season runs from 1 October to 31 December, and health authorities are warning this one could be busy. Victoria had its wettest winter since 2016 and its warmest on record, which means strong grass growth and more pollen when it flowers.

That matters because of thunderstorm asthma. When a storm hits on a high-pollen day, gusty winds can break pollen into tiny pieces that reach deep into the lungs. It can bring on sudden, severe asthma, even in people who have never had it.

10people died on 21 November 2016
3,300+extra emergency visits within 30 hours

On 21 November 2016, Melbourne had the world’s worst recorded thunderstorm asthma event. Ten people died, and more than 3,300 extra people turned up at emergency departments within 30 hours, according to Asthma Australia. Six of the ten who died were from Indian, Sri Lankan and South-East Asian backgrounds, the organisation said.

Research since then, summarised by University of Melbourne researchers, found people of Asian or Indian ancestry have a much higher risk of severe pollen-triggered asthma. Nearly two-thirds of people caught up in these events did not know they had asthma.

“Thunderstorm asthma can be life-threatening,” Victoria’s Chief Health Officer, Dr Caroline McElnay, said.

Why it matters to you

  • Hay fever counts. People with spring hay fever are at higher risk. If you sneeze every spring, see your GP before November.
  • Check the forecast. The VicEmergency app shows a three-day thunderstorm asthma risk (low, moderate or high) for each district. Set a watch zone for your area.
  • On high-risk days, get inside before the storm. The strong gusts before a storm are the danger. Close windows and doors, and turn off air conditioners that pull in outside air.
  • Keep your reliever handy and follow your asthma action plan. If you rely only on a reliever, ask your GP about a preventer.
  • Call 000 if someone is struggling to breathe or speak, is drowsy, or has blue lips.

Please share this with older relatives and anyone new to Melbourne. Many people who arrive from Sri Lanka have never experienced a Melbourne spring.

Sources: Victorian Department of Health, Epidemic thunderstorm asthma risk forecast; Victorian Government warning, as reported by Star Mail, 8 October 2026; Asthma Australia; University of Melbourne, Pursuit. General information, not medical advice.

item.title: The over-65 health rebate cut is blocked, for now
item.description: The Senate has pulled the private health bill off its agenda. The government says it will bring it straight back.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
The federal government’s plan to cut the private health insurance rebate for Australians aged 65 and over has stalled in the Senate. On Wednesday the Greens, the Coalition and independent senator Jacqui Lambie backed a motion to strike the bill from Parliament’s agenda, ABC News reported. Labor voted against the motion and was left on its own.

That means the bill cannot pass in its current form. It does not mean the idea is dead.

65+the age group whose rebate would have been cut
$3bnthe government expected to save over four years, for aged care
44,000people the government says would drop their cover
78,000the health department’s own forecast by the end of the decade

What the bill would have done

The change would have reduced the rebate for older Australians from April next year. About $1.6 billion of the savings was expected to come from pensioners. The government’s estimate is that 44,000 people would give up private cover. A health department analysis, released under Freedom of Information, forecast 78,000 by the end of the decade. Health Minister Mark Butler says the department treats 44,000 as the most reliable figure.

Where each side stands

The government says the savings are needed for aged care. Mr Butler called the Senate vote “an absolute travesty” and said he will reintroduce the same bill on Thursday.

The Coalition opposes the cut outright. Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston told the government to “drop it for good”.

The Greens say they support reducing private health rebates in principle, and would back the bill if pensioners were exempt.

What it means for your family

Nothing changes today, and nothing would have changed before April. If your parents or grandparents in Australia hold private cover, it is still worth knowing what they pay and what the rebate is worth to them. We will update this story when the bill returns.

Sources: ABC News, Stephanie Dalzell, 14 October 2026; ABC News, 12 October 2026. This is general information, not financial advice.

item.title: Rates up again: what 4.6% means for Melbourne households
item.description: The Reserve Bank has lifted rates for the fourth time this year. Here is what it costs, and why it happened.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
On 29 September the Reserve Bank of Australia raised the cash rate by a quarter of a percentage point, to 4.6%. It was the fourth rise of 2026 and the board’s decision was unanimous, The New Daily and AAP reported.

4.6%the cash rate after the 29 September decision
4rate rises in 2026 so far
$91extra a month on a typical $600,000 loan, from this rise alone
$364extra a month on the same loan since January, says Canstar

Why the RBA did it

The board pointed to inflation that is still too high, fresh disruption to global oil supply, and higher fuel prices feeding into the cost of other goods and services. In its statement it said “some of the upside risks to inflation are materialising”.

What it costs

If banks pass the rise on in full, the average variable rate for owner-occupiers goes to about 6.49%. On a $600,000 mortgage that is roughly $91 more a month. Canstar’s Sally Tindall said the bigger story is the total: “The true pain is in the cumulative impact.” By Canstar’s count, the same borrower pays about $364 a month more than at the start of the year.

If you have a loan

Check what your lender has done with your rate and when the new repayment starts. If money is tight, call your lender early; they have hardship options, and asking does not cost anything. The free National Debt Helpline (1800 007 007) can help you work through it.

Why it matters back home

Many Sri Lankan families in Melbourne also send money to Colombo every month. When repayments rise, that money is often the first thing squeezed, and families back home feel it too.

Sources: The New Daily / AAP, 29 September 2026, including figures from Canstar. This is general information, not financial advice.

item.title: Prices are rising 8% a year. Why the Central Bank is holding still
item.description: Inflation is at its highest in three years, driven by energy. The Central Bank has decided to wait.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
Prices in Colombo rose 8.0% in the year to September, the same as in August, according to figures from the Department of Census and Statistics released on 30 September. That is the Colombo Consumer Price Index, the measure most people mean when they talk about inflation.

8.0%headline inflation, September 2026
8.7%food inflation, up from 8.5% in August
8.75%the Central Bank’s policy rate, unchanged
5%the inflation target the Bank is aiming back towards

How we got here

Inflation has climbed through the year. It was 6.8% in June and 7.3% in July, which at the time was the highest reading since June 2023. The Central Bank says the main cause is an energy price shock, which then spreads into transport, food and almost everything else.

Why rates didn’t move

On the same day, 30 September, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka kept its Overnight Policy Rate at 8.75%. It raised rates by a full percentage point in May and says it wants to see how much of that has worked through before acting again. It also named tension in the Middle East and the risk of El Niño weather as reasons for caution.

The Bank expects inflation to stay in the high single digits until early 2027 and then ease back towards its 5% target. It says it will take a “forward-looking and data-dependent approach” and act if price pressures get worse.

What it means for you

If you live in Colombo, the weekly shop and the electricity bill are where you feel this most. If you send money home from Melbourne, the same rupees buy less than they did a year ago, so your family may need a little more to cover the same costs.

Sources: Department of Census and Statistics, CCPI, September 2026, as reported by Newswire, 30 September 2026; Central Bank of Sri Lanka policy decision, as reported by Newswire, 30 September 2026; Daily Mirror, 3 August 2026.

item.title: Budget 2027: the dates to know
item.description: The President presents the budget on 12 November. Here is how it moves through Parliament, and what economists are asking for.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
Sri Lanka’s 2027 budget has started its journey through Parliament. Deputy Minister of Finance Anil Jayantha tabled the Appropriation Bill on 7 October, Newswire reported. The bill sets out how much the government can spend next year; the budget speech explains what it will spend it on.

12 Novbudget speech by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, as Minister of Finance
20 Novsecond reading vote, 6pm
14 Decthird reading and final vote, 6pm
26days of debate in total

How it works

12 November: the President, who is also Minister of Finance, delivers the budget speech. This is when the tax and spending plans are announced.

13 to 20 November: seven days of debate on the budget as a whole, ending with the second reading vote. The government gets 60% of the speaking time and the opposition 40%.

21 November to 14 December: nineteen days of committee stage, where each ministry’s spending is debated. The split reverses, with the opposition getting 60%.

14 December: the final vote. Parliament will also sit on Saturdays during the debate, but not on Sundays or public holidays.

What economists are asking for

In September the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) urged the government to avoid both new tax rate rises and early tax cuts in this budget, and instead to widen the tax net and improve compliance, the Daily Mirror reported. Its argument is that Sri Lanka is at a delicate point in repairing its public finances.

We will explain the main announcements on the day of the speech.

Sources: Newswire, 7 October 2026; Sunday Times, 12 July 2026; Daily Mirror, 23 September 2026.

item.title: 1.7 million visitors so far, and Australians are near the top
item.description: Tourism is running slightly behind last year’s record. The busy winter season is about to start.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
More than 1.7 million tourists had visited Sri Lanka this year by 4 October, according to Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority figures reported by the Daily FT. That is 1,717,028 arrivals, about 2% behind the pace of 2025, which ended as a record year with 2.36 million.

1,717,028arrivals in 2026, to 4 October
~2%behind the same point in 2025
1,266Australians in the first four days of October, third after India and China
3mthe government’s original target for the year

Who is coming

India is by far the biggest market, with 447,476 visitors so far this year, followed by the UK and China. In the first four days of October, Australia was the third-largest source of visitors, with 1,266 arrivals, behind India and China.

Where it is heading

The government’s original target was 3 million visitors in 2026. The tourism authority’s revised forecasts now range from about 2.38 million to 2.60 million. At the lower end, that would only just beat last year’s record.

Heading home for the holidays?

The winter season, roughly December to March, is when hotels, flights and the south coast fill up. If you are planning a December trip from Melbourne, book early.

Source: Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority data, as reported by the Daily FT, 6 October 2026.

item.title: Lightning warnings: how to stay safe in a storm
item.description: The Met Department warned six provinces this week. Five simple rules from Sri Lanka Police.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
On Monday 13 October the Department of Meteorology issued an advisory for strong lightning in six provinces: Western, Sabaragamuwa, Central, Uva, North Western and Southern. It warned of thundery showers, mostly in the evening and at night, with strong winds at times.

Five rules for a lightning storm

Sri Lanka Police publishes this advice for severe lightning:

  • Get inside. Don’t stay outdoors or under trees. Shelter in a solid building or a closed vehicle.
  • Leave open ground. Keep away from paddy fields, tea estates, playgrounds and reservoirs.
  • Unplug. Don’t use corded phones or appliances that are plugged into the mains.
  • Skip the open ride. Avoid open vehicles such as bicycles, tractors and boats until it passes.
  • Watch for falling trees and wires. Strong winds can bring down trees and power lines.

Before you head out

Check the Department of Meteorology’s latest advisory, especially if you are travelling, working outdoors or have children walking home from school. In an emergency, contact your local disaster management office or the police.

Sources: Department of Meteorology advisory, 13 October 2026, as reported by TTV News; Sri Lanka Police lightning advisory. This is general safety information.

item.title: Dengue in 2026: over 100,000 cases so far
item.description: Sri Lanka is having a heavy dengue year. Most of what keeps it away is done at home, once a week.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
Sri Lanka has recorded 102,769 dengue cases so far this year, according to the National Dengue Control Unit, and 35 Medical Officer of Health (MOH) areas are under intensified surveillance as high-risk.

102,769dengue cases notified in 2026, National Dengue Control Unit
78deaths reported by 4 October
21,377cases in Gampaha, the worst-hit district, by 4 October
35high-risk MOH areas under intensified surveillance

Where it’s worst

The Western Province accounts for about half of all cases, with 52,906 by 4 October, The Morning reported, citing the National Dengue Control Unit. Gampaha has more cases than any other district.

The mosquito breeds in clean, still water. Usually yours.

What actually works

The dengue mosquito lays its eggs in small pools of clean water around homes, and it bites in the daytime. So the most useful habits are simple:

  • Once a week, empty and scrub anything that holds water: buckets, flower pots, plant trays, old tyres.
  • Clear roof gutters and any standing water in the garden.
  • Fit mesh screens on windows and vents.
  • Use insect repellent during the day, not just at night.

When to see a doctor

If you or your child has a fever for more than two days, see a doctor and ask about a dengue test. Use paracetamol for fever, and avoid painkillers like ibuprofen or aspirin unless a doctor says otherwise, as they can make bleeding worse with dengue. Get help straight away for severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding gums or unusual drowsiness.

Correction, 15 October 2026: we originally reported 82,838 cases to 7 October, 63 deaths, 17,600 cases in Gampaha, 175 high-risk areas and cases in 28 districts, from a newspaper’s dengue tracker. Those figures were out of date or wrong. We have replaced them with figures from the National Dengue Control Unit, removed the district count and weekly trend we could not confirm, and updated the headline.

Sources: National Dengue Control Unit, accessed 15 October 2026; The Morning, 4 October 2026, citing the National Dengue Control Unit. This is general information, not medical advice.

item.title: The rebate cut that could push 78,000 older Australians out of private cover
item.description: If your parents are over 65 and have private health insurance, this proposal is worth knowing about. It isn’t law yet.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
The federal government wants to wind back the private health insurance rebate for Australians aged 65 and over. It says the change would make rebates “fairer” and save about $3 billion to spend on aged care.

3.2mAustralians aged 65+ affected
44,000expected to drop cover in 2028–29
78,000expected to have dropped cover by the year after
$1.6bnof the savings expected to come from pensioners

Who it hits

More than 3.2 million older Australians would be affected, and about 2 million of them live on less than $37,000 a year. The health department’s own analysis, released under Freedom of Information, expects 44,000 people to drop their cover in 2028–29, rising to about 78,000 the following year. The department says those estimates are uncertain.

Will it happen?

Not yet. The Coalition says it will block the bill in the Senate, so the government needs the Greens. The Greens won’t support it as written and are looking at changes, such as exempting pensioners.

What to do now

Nothing changes today. If your parents rely on private cover, it’s worth knowing what they pay and what the rebate is worth to them, so the family isn’t caught out if the bill passes.

Update, 14 October: the Senate has pulled this bill off its agenda. The government says it will bring it back. Read the latest →

Source: ABC News, Stephanie Dalzell, 12 October 2026. This is general information, not financial advice.

item.title: Little Lanka: Sri Lankans in Melbourne, by the numbers
item.description: Half of all Sri Lanka-born Australians live in one city. One in five of them arrived in the last five years of the count.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
Walk through Dandenong, Clayton or Glen Waverley on a Saturday and you can buy hoppers, find a Buddhist temple, and hear Sinhala and Tamil in the same queue. The census explains why: Melbourne is the centre of Sri Lankan Australia.

65,152people in Greater Melbourne born in Sri Lanka
49%of all 131,904 Sri Lanka-born Australians
20%arrived between 2016 and 2021
42median age, against 37 for Melbourne overall

Who they are

Nearly half (48.6%) of Melbourne’s Sri Lanka-born residents are Buddhist. The most common type of work is professional, at 28% of those employed. Most speak another language at home as well as English, and arrivals have come in waves: the largest group, 29%, came between 2001 and 2010.

Two cities, one community. Most of it lives an hour from the CBD.

Why it matters for Colombo

This community doesn’t just live in Melbourne. It sends money home, flies back for weddings and funerals, and watches Sri Lanka’s economy from a distance. Many of the families who held on through the 2022 crisis did so with help from a relative abroad. We’ll be telling those stories from both ends.

Source: ABS 2021 Census, Greater Melbourne and Australia, people born in Sri Lanka. The share is our calculation from those figures. The 2026 Census results are due in 2027.

item.title: The money home: $8 billion and counting
item.description: Sri Lankans working abroad sent home a record US$8.07 billion in 2025. Here’s why that money matters more than almost any other.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
If you’re a Sri Lankan in Melbourne, you probably know the routine: a transfer home at the end of the month, for parents, a sibling’s school fees, a roof repair. Multiply that by hundreds of thousands of people around the world, and you get one of the biggest sources of dollars Sri Lanka has.

$8.07bnworkers’ remittances in 2025, a record
+22.8%up from US$6.57 billion in 2024
$7.24bnthe old record, set in 2016
$879mDecember 2025, the biggest single month ever

Why it matters

Remember the dollar jar from our explainer on the 2022 default? Sri Lanka needs dollars to buy fuel, medicine and food from abroad. Money sent home by workers overseas goes straight into that jar. When remittances slowed during the crisis, the jar emptied faster. Now they’re at a record, and they’re one reason the recovery has held.

Every transfer home is a small loan to the whole country’s dollar jar.

What the number doesn’t show

These figures count money sent through banks and formal channels. They don’t say how much comes from Australia in particular, and they don’t show what it costs the people sending it. If you send money home from Melbourne, we’d like to hear your story: info@thedosagemag.com.

Source: Central Bank of Sri Lanka figures, as reported by Ada Derana Biz (January 2026). All figures in US dollars.

item.title: The $3 billion deal, explained
item.description: What Sri Lanka’s IMF programme is, what it asked for, and what happens when it ends in March 2027.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
After the 2022 default, Sri Lanka needed two things: dollars, and a plan that would make lenders trust it again. The International Monetary Fund offered both, with conditions attached.

~$3bnthe programme’s total size, over 48 months
20 Mar 2023the date the IMF approved it
~$2.4bnpaid out so far, after the latest reviews in May 2026
Mar 2027when it ends, with two reviews still to go

How it works

The money doesn’t arrive in one go. It comes in slices. Every few months, IMF staff check Sri Lanka’s progress, and if the country has kept its promises, the next slice is released. In May 2026, after the fifth and sixth reviews, the latest slice was about US$695 million.

What Sri Lanka promised

In plain terms: collect more tax, spend within limits, fix the electricity sector so it stops losing money, and keep prices stable. From 2027, the government must run a primary surplus of 2.3% of GDP, meaning it takes in more than it spends before paying interest on its debts. That’s why taxes and electricity bills went up, and why many families felt the recovery as a squeeze.

The IMF doesn’t just lend money. It lends credibility, and charges for it in reforms.

What comes next

As of June, no talks had started on a new programme. The IMF said Sri Lanka’s engagement after this one is “yet to be discussed,” while some economists say the country will likely need another. The IMF itself still calls the risks to Sri Lanka’s debt “high.”

Sources: Daily Mirror (May 2026); Daily Mirror (June 2026). The total is SDR 2.286 billion; dollar figures are approximate.

item.title: Sri Lanka’s first pickleball league serves on Friday
item.description: Eight franchises, a player auction and a cricketer in the owners’ box. The Ceylon Pickle League runs 16 to 18 October at the Colombo Pickle Club.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
Less than three years after the first courts opened in Moratuwa, pickleball in Sri Lanka is getting a professional league. The Ceylon Pickle League, the country’s first franchise competition in the sport, plays its opening season this Friday to Sunday at the Colombo Pickle Club on Torrington Avenue.

8franchise teams, all sold before the league launched
5categories, from men’s singles to masters doubles
3days of play, 16 to 18 October
2024the year Sri Lanka’s first courts opened

How it works

The league borrows the model cricket fans know from the IPL and LPL. Owners buy a franchise, players go through selection and an auction, and teams carry a city’s name. The eight are the Colombo Aces, Kandy Knights, Galle Kings, Trinco Titans, Yarl Dinkers, Ella Archers, Bentota Nyners and Weligama Sharks. They compete across men’s doubles, women’s doubles, mixed doubles, men’s singles and masters doubles, and players from India are expected in the first edition.

It is run by Eventistry Sports with the Colombo Pickle Club. Sampath Bank is the title partner, and matches will be shown on PEO TV, produced by KSN Live.

“CPL is about far more than pickleball.” Karin Wijeratne, founder, Eventistry Sports

A fast bowler buys in

The best-known owner is Matheesha Pathirana, the Sri Lanka fast bowler, whose first franchise investment is the Yarl Dinkers. “This is more than just a team. It is an idea I truly believe in,” he said when the deal was announced in August.

Why now

Pickleball arrived here in early 2024. By this year, a guide to the island’s courts listed 20 places to play, from Nugegoda to Negombo. “Pickleball has been growing incredibly fast around the world,” said Subraja Subramaniam, co-founder of the Colombo Pickle Club, at the league’s launch in May. The organisers are betting Sri Lanka is ready to follow: a sport that is quick to learn, works for every age, and now has teams to support.

Going

Tickets are sold through the league’s website, ceylonpickleleague.com. New to the sport? Read our guide first: Pickleball has found Colombo.

Sources: Ceylon Pickle League; The Morning (May 2026); Daily FT (June 2026); Sunday Times (June 2026); ThePapare (August 2026).

item.title: Pickleball has found Colombo
item.description: Two years after the first courts opened, the paddle sport is everywhere from Nugegoda to Negombo. Here’s how it works, and where to play.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
In January 2024, a club called Pipinya opened a handful of courts in Moratuwa for a sport most Sri Lankans had never heard of. That April it hosted what it called the country’s first pickleball tournament, open to every age and skill level. Two and a half years later, you can book a court on a weeknight in Colombo 07, Rajagiriya, Battaramulla, Nugegoda, Negombo or by the beach in Ahangama.

2024the year the first courts opened in Sri Lanka
20venues listed in a 2026 guide to the island’s courts
Rs 2–5kwhat most venues charge for a court, per hour
11points to win a game (by two)

What it actually is

Think tennis, shrunk to a badminton-sized court and played with a solid paddle and a light plastic ball full of holes. The ball moves slower than a tennis ball, so rallies last longer and beginners can keep up within one session. Most games are doubles.

The rules fit on a napkin. Serve underarm, diagonally. Let the ball bounce once on each side before anyone volleys. Stay out of “the kitchen,” the strip next to the net, when hitting the ball out of the air. Only the serving team scores, and the first to 11 wins, as long as they’re two points clear.

Easy to learn in an hour. Hard to put down after that.

Why it’s spreading

In the United States it has been named the fastest-growing sport for four years running, with nearly 20 million people playing in 2024. Here, the appeal is simpler. It’s social, it mixes ages, an hour after work is enough, and courts are cheaper to build than tennis courts, which is why they keep appearing in car parks, rooftops and old warehouses.

Where to start

Most venues lend paddles and balls and run beginner sessions, so you don’t need to buy anything first. Book an off-peak slot, bring three friends, and split the court fee. If you play outdoors, go early or late: the ball is light, and so is your patience in the midday sun.

Sources: The Morning (April 2024), Daily Mirror (November 2024), pickle.lk court guide (2026), SFIA via Pickleball.com. Prices vary by venue and time; check before you book.

item.title: The cinnamon in your kitchen probably isn’t ours
item.description: Most cinnamon sold around the world is cassia. Ceylon cinnamon is a different spice, and Europe now protects its name.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
Pick up a jar labelled “cinnamon” in a supermarket in Melbourne, London or Dubai, and there’s a good chance it isn’t what grows in Sri Lanka. It’s usually cassia: a close relative, grown mostly in China, Vietnam and Indonesia, that is cheaper, stronger and darker.

Two spices, one name

Ceylon cinnamon (Cinnamomum verum) is peeled from the inner bark and rolled by hand into thin, papery layers, like a cigar. It’s light tan, crumbles easily, and tastes sweet and delicate. Cassia is a single thick, hard curl of bark: darker, harsher and spicier.

~100×more coumarin in cassia than in Ceylon cinnamon
6 mgsafe daily coumarin limit for a 60 kg adult
~2 gof the strongest cassia tested reaches that limit
2022the year the EU protected the name “Ceylon cinnamon”

Why it matters for your health

Cassia contains a natural compound called coumarin, which in large amounts can harm the liver. Europe’s food safety authority sets a tolerable limit of 0.1 mg per kilo of body weight per day, which is 6 mg for a 60 kg adult. Austria’s food agency measured cassia at 1,880 to 3,260 mg of coumarin per kilo, and the highest Ceylon sample at 185 mg. By our calculation, about 2 grams of the strongest cassia, less than a teaspoon, reaches the daily limit. You’d need more than 30 grams of Ceylon cinnamon to do the same.

Same name on the jar. A hundred times the coumarin.

A name worth protecting

In February 2022, the European Union recognised Ceylon cinnamon as a protected geographical indication, the first for any Sri Lankan product. Only cinnamon grown and processed here, the traditional way, can be sold in the EU under that name. Mexico, where cinnamon goes into churros, hot chocolate and café de olla, is another loyal buyer: cinnamon tops the list of what Sri Lanka sells there.

How to tell at home

Look for “Ceylon cinnamon” or Cinnamomum verum on the label. Check the sticks: many thin layers rolled together means Ceylon; one thick hollow tube means cassia. And if you’re in Sri Lanka, you’re already in the right place.

Sources: AGES, Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety; UNIDO; Sri Lanka Export Development Board. This is general information, not medical advice.

item.title: The two-minute walk after dinner
item.description: A short stroll after eating blunts the blood sugar spike. You don’t need a gym, or even ten minutes.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
After a plate of rice and curry, the natural move is the sofa. A growing body of research suggests getting up for a few minutes instead is one of the simplest things you can do for your blood sugar.

2–5minutes of light walking per break in the studies
17%lower blood sugar with light walking, compared with sitting
9.5%lower with standing breaks alone
60–90minutes after eating, when blood sugar tends to peak

What the research found

In 2022, researchers at the University of Limerick pulled together seven studies comparing three things: sitting for long stretches, breaking that up by standing, and breaking it up with light walking. Participants took short breaks of two to five minutes, every 20 to 30 minutes across the day.

Standing helped: blood sugar was about 9.5% lower on average than with prolonged sitting. Light walking helped more, at about 17% lower, and blood sugar and insulin also rose and fell more gently. The walking was not exercise in the gym sense. It was a stroll.

Not a workout. A stroll.

How to fit it in

Because blood sugar tends to peak within an hour or so of a meal, the best time to move is soon after eating. Walk to the end of the lane and back. Do a few laps of the garden. Take the stairs. Wash up standing, then take your phone call on foot. At the office, a two-minute walk every half hour does the same job.

It’s not a replacement for medication or a doctor’s advice, especially if you have diabetes. But it’s free, it takes two minutes, and you can start tonight.

Source: Buffey et al., Sports Medicine (2022), a meta-analysis of seven studies, as reported by CNN. This is general information, not medical advice.

item.title: The Dosage is back
item.description: One story per edition, told in full. Printed to keep, with everything else a scan away.
item.dc:creator: Eashaan Dassanayaka
item.content:encoded:
We went quiet. Sri Lanka didn't. Since The Dosage last published, the country has been through a fuel crisis, a default and a long, uneven recovery. We've come back to report it properly.

The new Dosage works differently. Each edition is one story, followed all the way through, instead of fifty short pieces. It's printed as a slim, collectible edition. Point your phone at any page and the story opens up: the film, the voices, and the numbers explained simply.

What's next

Edition 01 is in the works. Until then, we'll be publishing regular stories about Sri Lanka here: explainers, the numbers behind the headlines, and the people living them.

Follow us on Instagram, Facebook and YouTube to be first to see the launch date.

Reality, unfiltered.

item.title: Sri Lanka's recovery, in four numbers
item.description: The World Bank says the economy is back. The same report shows why many families don't feel it.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
In October 2026 the World Bank published its latest update on Sri Lanka, titled From Recovery to Transformation. Read the headline and the story is good. Read further and a second story appears.

12straight quarters of economic growth
4.4%growth forecast for 2026, up from 3.6% in April
~12%how far real wages remain below 2019
15.8%of people below the $4.20-a-day poverty line in 2026, against 11.5% in 2019

Why both are true

Growth measures the size of the whole economy. It can rise while wages, measured against prices, stay below where they were. Prices are also moving again: headline inflation reached 8% in August, even though the Bank expects it to average 5.7% for the year.

The country is recovering faster than the people inside it.

Source: World Bank, Sri Lanka Development Update (October 2026), as reported by the Daily FT.

item.title: What happens when a country can't pay?
item.description: Explained simply: the dollar jar, the default, and why the fuel queues began.
item.dc:creator: The Dosage
item.content:encoded:
You've probably heard that Sri Lanka "ran out of money" in 2022. That isn't quite right. It had rupees, and could print more. What it ran out of was dollars.

The dollar jar

Sri Lanka buys fuel, medicine and many foods from abroad, and the sellers want dollars. So the country keeps a jar of them: its foreign reserves. Tourism, exports and money sent home by Sri Lankans abroad fill the jar. Repaying foreign loans empties it.

When tourism collapsed in the pandemic and loan repayments kept coming, the jar ran low. Ships carrying fuel waited offshore to be paid, and queues formed at every station.

The default

In April 2022 Sri Lanka told its foreign lenders it would stop repaying them for now. That is a default. Picture a family announcing at a wedding that it can't pay back any relative this year: everyone hears, and nobody lends again until there's a plan.

A default isn't a technicality. It's the moment the whole world stops lending.

The plan came later, through an IMF programme and a long negotiation with lenders. We'll explain each of those steps in the next stories in this series.

An explainer by The Dosage.

item.title: Breaking the status quo with Jeana De Zoysa
item.description: On the banks of Bolgoda, Jeana De Zoysa, activist, wildlife guide and old friend, explains why changing the world starts with changing what we treat as normal.
item.dc:creator: Dassa Vlogs · Episode 13
item.content:encoded:
Editor’s Travels · Dassa Vlogs Ep 13
Photo: Extract and Design

Breaking the status quo with Jeana De Zoysa

From the archiveThis story is based on a film first published on Dassa Vlogs on 5 August 2020, while The Dosage was on hold. Jeana’s roles, projects and views are as they were at the time of filming.

The last time Eashaan Dassanayaka and Jeana De Zoysa properly caught up, she was leaving for Malaysia and he for Australia. Five or six years on, in the middle of 2020, they sat down beside Bolgoda lake in Panadura to fill in the gaps.

Five or six years later

A lot had happened. Jeana had finished a bachelor’s degree in arts and social sciences, majoring in global studies. She’d travelled, thrown herself into environmental activism, and helped organise campaigns and protests. By the time of filming she was working as a freelance field guide in Yala, running social media for the wild-cat conservation group SCAR, and helping launch Earthly, an app where environmental groups post their projects and find volunteers.

The lockdown, she said, had been hard on everyone. “I’m constantly having to remind myself that I’ve been in a really lucky and privileged position.”

Eco-feminist, anarcho-primitivist

Her Instagram bio describes her as both, so Eashaan asked what that means. Eco-feminism, she explained, links the way women are held down under patriarchy with the way nature is exploited under the same systems. Anarcho-primitivism is harder to sell. Anarchy, she says, isn’t chaos and looting: “Anarchy very simply is the antithesis of hierarchy,” a world of self-governance without class systems. The primitivism part is the belief that humankind needs to return to simpler ways of living. “That’s a pretty unpopular belief,” she admits.

Rebellion, Sri Lankan style

Extinction Rebellion began in the UK in 2018 and spread fast. Jeana had wanted to start a Sri Lankan branch, went travelling, and came back four months later to find one already running. She joined, became its spokesperson and later a national coordinator. The group ran reforestation drives, beach clean-ups, education work and protests.

Eashaan pushed her on a common complaint: plenty of people call themselves activists on Instagram without doing much. She agreed that people should “walk the walk”, but said it starts with talking. “It’s about trying your best and acknowledging the choices that we have, and making the most conscious and compassionate choice.” She’s honest about it, too: “I’m still a hypocrite in a lot of ways.”

We have to really unlearn and re-evaluate how we live our lives.

Going vegan

Jeana went vegetarian four years before the film and spent the following year phasing out dairy and eggs. For her it’s a whole lifestyle: food, products, clothes. Her reason was simple. “My whole life I absolutely loved animals. I deemed myself a conservationist,” she said. “There was just a moment when I woke up and realised I can’t call myself these things while I still contribute to these industries.”

“What’s the difference between a dog and a pig and a chicken or a cow or a leopard?” she asks. “They’re all sentient. They all value their lives.” She also points to the environmental case, arguing that animal farming is a major driver of emissions, water use and deforestation, and makes a health case too.

Eashaan shares his own story: he first heard the word “vegan” working in a restaurant in Australia, when a customer asked for a vegan platter. Curious, he ended up at a gathering of environmental activists around a fire, listening to punk rock and asking how they managed it all.

This film was sponsored by The Vegan Kade, which brought in vegan products that are hard to find in Sri Lanka and sold them through its Instagram and Facebook pages.

▶ Watch the film · 30 min

Breaking the status quo with Jeana De Zoysa

Zero waste and the dress from Grandma

Beyond diet, Jeana talks about zero waste (“you can’t do it overnight”), minimalism and buying local. Instead of a plastic bottle of Coca-Cola, she suggests, drink straight from a coconut. She hadn’t bought new clothes in about three years: her dress was a hand-me-down, altered by her grandmother. Eashaan points out his own shirt is his dad’s, 20 years old. “See, you can look cool and not be spending your money and destroying the environment.”

The animals with no protection

The conversation turns to animal welfare. Jeana had protested a Colombo plan to round up stray dogs into shelters, which she says leaves weaker dogs to be attacked and spreads disease. Bigger than that, she says, Sri Lanka’s animal-protection law dates back more than a century, and animal cruelty can be punished with a fine of just 100 rupees. An Animal Welfare Bill was drafted in 2006 and, as of the film, still hadn’t passed.

Update, 2026Cabinet approved a new Animal Welfare Bill in June 2026 and it was gazetted in July, with fines of up to Rs 250,000 and jail terms for cruelty. It still has to pass Parliament. Explainer · The bill

Three small cats

At SCAR, Small Cat Advocacy & Research, Jeana ran the social media. The group works to raise the profile of Sri Lanka’s three small wild cats, the fishing cat, the jungle cat and the rusty-spotted cat, which get far less attention than the leopard. On safari, she says, people chase the big five and miss everything else: “the flowers and the small dung beetles and the insect life, the bird life.”

She’s careful not to blame villagers for the snares that kill leopards. Many are farmers protecting their crops or catching bushmeat to feed their families, and, she says, part of the demand comes from “privileged people from Colombo” ordering wild meat on safari.

Changing the status quo

Asked about the future, Jeana wanted to keep guiding, to “spark that inner conservationist” in visitors, and to go back to study, this time science, to help fill the gaps in research on Sri Lanka’s wildlife.

In the end, she says, our power is in how we choose to live. “That inspires the people around us, and the domino effect.” Her closing line is an old one, but she means it: be the change you want to see in the world.

  • Earthly, Sri Lanka’s free app for environmental volunteering
  • The Vegan Kade, the film’s sponsor
  • The Vegan Society’s guide to going vegan

item.title: The Sri Lankan Bartender behind Colombo's forbidden Love story
item.description: A chance meeting with an old school friend at a door in Colombo 7, almost six years after they last saw each other.
item.dc:creator: Dassa Vlogs · Episode 11
item.content:encoded:
Editor’s Travels · Dassa Vlogs Ep 11
Photo: Sebastian Olegard

The Sri Lankan Bartender behind Colombo's forbidden Love story

From the archiveThis story is based on a film first published on Dassa Vlogs on 9 June 2020, while The Dosage was on hold. Names, places and details are as they were at the time of filming.

In March 2020, Eashaan Dassanayaka landed back in Sri Lanka. Weeks later, he walked up to the front door of a bar in Colombo 7 and found Vimuth Joseph standing there. The two had been at school together. The last time they’d seen each other was almost six years earlier.

The reunion

What started as a hello at the door turned into an evening of catching up, with a camera rolling.

▶ Watch the film

The Sri Lankan Bartender behind Colombo's forbidden Love story

Almost six years apart, and then a hello at the door.

Behind the camera

Unlike his other vlogs, Eashaan invested real time in this one. He brought in a small crew so viewers could see the place and the people the way they deserved. A one-minute teaser went out on 4 June 2020, and the full 13-minute episode followed on 9 June.

It was a non-profit video, made for the love of the story.
